Let me start by understanding the situation better. My best friend, who's 21, went on a three-month trip to India to do volunteer work. He helped build a water pipeline and taught kids about hygiene and sanitation. That's really impressive! Plus, he paid for the entire trip himself, which cost over $3000. I know he didn't tell many people about the trip before he left, and I'm not sure if he would have told people when he got back if I hadn't done this. I thought he needed recognition for the great work he did, so I decided to make a Facebook post about him to let all his friends and family know about the trip. I made the post while he was away, about a week before he got home. Because of where he was, he didn't have any internet connection, so he didn't see my post until he started traveling home. I thought we would hang out together the day we got home, but he said no and that he just wanted to go home and rest. I decided to text him that evening to ask again what was wrong. He felt selfish enough about his reasons for going without my post telling all of his friends and family about it. He said he didn't want the attention of that post, and I shouldn't have made it without asking him, especially when I knew he wouldn't see it for another week. I was kind of annoyed at him because I thought I was doing a really nice thing, since he would be too shy to tell people about it himself. The post was so positive about him; I didn't say anything bad. So, the question is: AITA (Am I The Ass) for making that post? First, I need to consider the moral aspects of this situation. Making a Facebook post about someone without their consent can be seen as an invasion of their privacy. Even though the intention was positive, it's important to respect the other person's wishes and boundaries. My friend is shy and didn't tell many people about the trip. He went on the trip for self-improvement and didn't want attention for it. By making the post, I went against his desire for privacy and attention. Even though I thought it was a nice thing to do, it's not okay to make decisions for someone else about how they want to be perceived. Additionally, I knew he wouldn't see the post for another week, which means I didn't give him the chance to consent or object before posting it. This lack of communication is a key issue here. On the other hand, I did think he needed recognition for his good work, and I wanted to share his achievements with others. However, this should have been done in a way that respects his privacy and wishes. In conclusion, while my intentions were good, the action of making the Facebook post without his consent was not morally acceptable. It's important to respect others' boundaries and communicate before sharing personal information about them.
